newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean steelmaker founders in new blow to economy.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean steelmaker founders in new blow to economy.

text.p: Another South Korean steel company filed for court receivership on Tuesday, dealing a new blow to the ailing banking system and raising fears of a domino effect as the economy slows.
Sammi Steel Co sought protection from its creditors on Tuesday along with four other affiliates of Sammi Group, the country's 26th-biggest conglomerate.
It was the second steel maker to founder this year after Hanbo Steel Co folded under $5.8 billion of debt in January in the country's biggest bankruptcy.
The news sent share prices on the Seoul stock exchange tumbling on Wednesday, partly on worries that tighter credit as a result of the failures could push other indebted companies over the edge.
The leading index lost 1.78 percent, or 11.68 points, to close at 646.29.
"There is a good possibility of further bankruptcies coming on line," said Lim Chun-soo, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Capital Markets Ltd.

Sammi's troubles were a fresh blow to the economy, officially forecast to grow at 6.0 percent this year against around 7.0 percent last year. Some economists predict growth could slow to 5.0 percent, the lowest since 1980.
Benchmark three-year interest rates edged up to close at an 18-month high of 12.85 percent from 12.75 percent on Tuesday on fears that liquidity could dry up further.

The won continued to slide, propelled by renewed concerns that the latest corporate crisis would reduce the inflow of foreign lending and squeeze the supply of dollars. The won ended at 884.60, down from Tuesday close of 883.10.
The won has fallen by about 12 percent since the start of last year, slashing corporate profits by raising the burden of overseas debt servicing costs.
Sammi Steel had liabilities of 1.45 trillion won ($1.6 billion) at the end of 1996 against assets of 1.53 trillion won, according to company figures.
Korea First Bank is Sammi Steel's biggest creditor, with 395.9 billion won of outstanding loans at the end of 1996. The bank issued a statement saying it would seek a buyer for the stricken firm.
Korea First Bank is also the biggest lender to Hanbo Steel. Last month the bank's long-term debt rating was lowered by Moody's Investors Service.

Sammi Steel has been struggling under debt repayments and falling prices for stainless steel products. In calendar 1996, it posted a net loss of 119.98 billion won against a loss of 39.45 billion in 1995.
Trading in shares of Sammi Steel and its marketing affiliate Sammi Corp was halted.
Sammi Metal Products Co, Sammi Technology and Industries Co and Sammi Fine Ceramics Co -- the other troubled units of Sammi Group -- are not listed.
At a news conference, Sammi group chairman Kim Hyun-bae said he was confident the group would recover after selling property and other assets.
"I am confident we will achieve business normalisation in a fairly short period of time," he said.
Kim said property sales would take time to complete. In the meantime, the group could not handle rising financing costs and faced difficulty securing fresh loans.

South Korea's banking system was shaken by the Hanbo failure, which exposed weak credit analysis and corrupt lending practices. Three top bankers are now on trial for bribery in a loans scandal linked to the collapse.
